target_customer: Amputees buying custom prosthetic legs, later prosthetics clinics using socket design software, then computer vision developers
problem: Custom prosthetic legs cost thousands of dollars and take long to make. Standard Cyborg started with 3D printed legs at a low price and moved to scanning and socket design software.
business_model: Direct sales of 3D printed prostheses, then software for clinics, then a computer vision platform

founders.name: Jeff Huber
education: North Carolina State University, dropped out
founders.background_notes: TechCrunch (Feb 2015) calls him the sole founder and employee; he was born without a fully formed fibula and previously worked in education and advertising.

exit.reason: Össur bought the Design Studio prosthetics software rights in May 2020 and the company said it was building a broader computer vision platform. The site later says the company has been retired.

competitors.name: Hanger Prosthetics and Orthotics
competitors.what: Austin-based incumbent prosthetics provider, founded more than 150 years earlier
competitors.traction_then: Roughly a quarter of the market per TechCrunch

technical_complexity.rationale: Fitting and manufacturing 3D printed prosthetics with carbon fiber reinforcement involves biomechanics and clinical fit, and the later computer vision platform needed machine learning infrastructure.

defensibility.rationale: Scanning and socket design software used by about a dozen clinics gave some workflow stickiness, but the original printed legs were easy to copy and clinics held the customer relationship.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Össur bought the Design Studio software rights in May 2020. No source shows incumbents copying the original 3D printed legs.

market_need_then: TechCrunch cited a market dominated by a century-old incumbent with high prices, versus a 499 dollar printed leg. The founder's own experience as an amputee supplied the personal pain point.

branding.domain_note: Used standardcyborg.com; the site now only says the company has been retired and links to GitHub.

identity.voice_and_tone: Mission language about making computer vision accessible

branding.community_and_virality: Open source projects on GitHub linked from its site

brand_strength.rationale: Coverage by TechCrunch, Business Insider and Fortune was about the product and founder story, not the brand. The cyborg name suits prosthetics but did not fit the later computer vision platform.

pivots.why: Fortune (May 2016) reports clinics were already using its software; the shift reason is not stated
The company's May 2020 post says it focused on a broader platform by 2019 and sought a new owner for Design Studio

outcome_analysis: Standard Cyborg began as a one founder YC Winter 2015 company selling low cost printed legs, moved to clinic software in 2016, sold its Design Studio to Össur in May 2020 and tried to become a computer vision platform before going inactive. Funding reported at 2M in 2018 and small other rounds did not carry the pivot to a stand-alone outcome. No post-mortem states the cause, so the failure factors are inferred from the pivots and the sale of the core business and are tentative.
notes: Funding sources conflict: CB Insights shows about 240K over three rounds with a 120K seed in March 2019 (Hustle Fund), while startupintros reports a 2M seed in December 2018 with named angels. The 2M round rests on that single tracker and the 120K round on a single database. The 200K angel round comes from a 3dprinting.com headline seen in search results only (date and investors unknown, page not opened). A Praxis profile snippet says Garrett Spiegel co-founded the company; that page was not opened, so he is not listed as a founder. Exit type is unknown because the company sold only its prosthetics software, while YC lists Inactive. A company post on the sale and a Notion page by someone who ran the final process were not opened successfully.
